add-feature.description: Plan a new feature through simple questions
add-feature.template: Help a beginner add a feature to an existing app. Feature idea: $ARGUMENTS. Read existing project context, plans, and relevant code. Ask exactly ONE nontechnical question at a time, offering clear choices, a recommendation where sensible, 'I'm not sure', and custom answers. Ask about what the user wants to accomplish, who uses it, what they see, what information is needed, how success works, and unusual situations. Do not ask the user to choose APIs, database schemas, or implementation patterns. Avoid repeated questions. Summarize the proposed behavior and get approval. Then write a detailed implementation plan in .agents/plans/ with acceptance criteria, technical tasks, tests, and dependency-ordered checklist items with blockers (or None). Update .agents/context/FEATURES.md to reflect planned status. Do not implement. Suggest /build-app next.

change-feature.description: Plan changes to something already in the app
change-feature.template: Help a beginner change an existing feature. Request: $ARGUMENTS. Inspect the feature and relevant project documentation. Explain its current behavior in everyday language. Ask exactly ONE simple question at a time, with choices and a custom option, until the desired behavior and consequences are clear. Preserve unrelated behavior. Summarize changes, get approval, and create a dependency-ordered plan in .agents/plans/ including tests and acceptance criteria. Update context as appropriate. Do not implement yet; suggest /build-app.

fix-problem.description: Explain and fix an application problem
fix-problem.template: Help a beginner troubleshoot a problem without requiring technical terms. Problem description: $ARGUMENTS. Inspect code and available error output. If necessary, ask ONE simple question at a time about what they did, what they expected, and what happened; offer choices when useful. Reproduce or verify the issue when practical, find the likely cause, and make the smallest safe fix. For risky or major behavior changes, explain the impact and request approval first. Run relevant tests or checks, document unresolved issues, and update .agents/progress/STATUS.md. Do not push or deploy. Explain the fix and how the user can check it in plain language.

review-app.description: Check the application for problems and improvements
review-app.template: Review the existing app against approved plans and .agents/context. Focus on missing features, broken flows, usability, accessibility, security basics, and test coverage. Request: $ARGUMENTS. Run read-only checks where practical. Present a short beginner-friendly report grouped into working well, needs attention, and optional improvements. Prioritize issues and suggest concrete next commands. Do not implement changes, push code, or modify production. Clearly distinguish verified findings from suggestions.

project-status.description: See what's finished and what to do next
project-status.template: Read .agents/context, .agents/plans, .agents/progress/STATUS.md, and repository state. Explain in plain language what the application does, what has been finished, what is in progress, any blockers, and the ONE best next step. Do not assume checklist items are complete without evidence. If status files are missing, inspect the code and say what can and cannot be confirmed. Do not modify files. User question: $ARGUMENTS.

explain.description: Explain any part of the app in simple words
explain.template: Explain this topic to a complete beginner: $ARGUMENTS. Use project context and code when relevant. Start with a simple answer, use a real-world analogy if helpful, define unavoidable technical words, and give an example from their app. Ask one clarifying question only if necessary. Do not modify files.

guide.description: Find the next best step for your application
guide.template: Act as a friendly project guide. Read project files, .agents/context, .agents/plans, .agents/progress/STATUS.md, and available commands in opencode.json or opencode.jsonc. User's situation: $ARGUMENTS. Identify the current stage: no project, idea only, needs requirements, needs design, approved plan ready to build, unfinished build, review needed, or ongoing maintenance. Recommend ONE best next command with an exact copyable example and a brief explanation. If the state is unclear, ask ONE simple multiple-choice question. Never invent commands or automatically execute them. Do not modify files.

forgot.description: Find the right command by describing what you want
forgot.template: The user is a beginner who forgot which command to use. Their goal: $ARGUMENTS. Read the current OpenCode configuration to discover actual available commands and descriptions. Recommend ONE best matching command (at most two if genuinely ambiguous), show the exact command including their request when useful, and explain in one or two plain-language sentences. If unclear, ask ONE question with choices. Never invent commands, execute commands, or modify files.

help-me.template: Read the project's actual OpenCode configuration and list its available custom commands. Group them under Starting, Building, Improving, Fixing, GitHub, and Getting Help. For each, show its exact name and a very short everyday-language description. If the user provides a goal ($ARGUMENTS), highlight the most relevant command. End by suggesting /forgot followed by what they want to do. Do not invent commands or modify files.

test.description: Run available tests and explain failures
test.template: Run the relevant test suite and coverage report if the project supports coverage. Request: $ARGUMENTS. Report which commands ran, which checks passed or failed, and any coverage results that actually exist. Explain failures in plain language and suggest fixes; do not invent coverage numbers. Do not change code unless explicitly requested.

push.description: Commit and push approved changes to main
push.template: Help a beginner save intended changes to GitHub main. Request: $ARGUMENTS. Inspect repository status, branch, remote, staged/unstaged files, and ahead/behind status. Review changes for secrets, .env files, credentials, generated artifacts, and unrelated files; stage only appropriate files. If on a branch other than main, if there are unrelated changes, or if integrating remote changes is necessary, stop and ask before switching, merging, or moving work. Run relevant checks when feasible. Explain the files and destination, and obtain explicit confirmation before committing and pushing to origin/main. Generate a meaningful commit message, commit only intended changes, and push without force. Respect branch protection. If there is nothing to commit but local commits to push, explain them and confirm before pushing. Report actual success or failure in simple terms. Never force push, discard work, or deploy.

push-pr.description: Create a feature branch and open a GitHub pull request
push-pr.template: Help a beginner submit changes for review. Request: $ARGUMENTS. Inspect Git status, branch, remotes, commit history, and existing pull requests when possible. Determine intended files and commits; exclude secrets and unrelated work. Avoid duplicate PRs. If creating a branch from the current state would include unrelated commits or dirty work cannot be safely isolated, explain and ask before proceeding. Fetch origin/main when available. Choose a descriptive unique branch name (feature/... or fix/...), preserve intended changes, run relevant checks, and prepare a meaningful commit and PR title/body with summary and test results. Before publishing changes or opening the PR, show the branch, intended changes, target main, and ask for explicit confirmation. Then push without force and create the PR with authenticated gh CLI or a supported GitHub integration. Do not merge automatically. If authentication or permissions are missing, explain what is needed; never claim a PR was created unless confirmed. Return the real PR URL if successful.

push-changes.description: Legacy alias for saving changes to GitHub
push-changes.template: This is the legacy push-changes command. Follow the same safe workflow as /push: inspect repository and intended changes, exclude secrets, explain destination, obtain explicit confirmation, commit appropriate files, and push to origin/main without force. Do not switch branches or integrate commits without consent. User request: $ARGUMENTS.

start-build.description: Start or continue building the app from an approved plan

design-this.description: Design your app using screenshots or visual inspiration
design-this.template: Act as a professional UI/UX designer helping a complete beginner design their application. User request: $ARGUMENTS. Ask the user to upload or paste one or more screenshots of designs they like, unless screenshots are already provided. Accept screenshots from websites, mobile apps, Pinterest, Dribbble, Figma, or other visual references. Analyze the screenshots carefully, identifying colors, typography, spacing, layout, navigation, cards, buttons, forms, icons, borders, shadows, and overall visual style. Read .agents/context, .agents/plans, and relevant project code to understand the application's purpose, existing pages, components, and frontend framework. Explain the visual style in simple, nontechnical language. Ask exactly ONE beginner-friendly question at a time, offering clear choices, a recommendation, 'I'm not sure', and a custom answer. Ask only questions needed to clarify which visual elements the user likes, which parts should be adapted, and whether the design should apply to the whole app or specific pages. Do not ask the user to choose CSS frameworks, component libraries, or implementation patterns. Recommend sensible defaults based on the screenshots and existing project. Treat inspiration as a reference rather than requiring an exact copy. Preserve the application's functionality and adapt the design to its own branding and content. Create a reusable design system covering color tokens, typography, spacing, layout, responsive breakpoints, navigation, buttons, inputs, cards, tables, dialogs, icons, loading states, empty states, error states, accessibility, and mobile behavior where applicable. Reuse existing design tools and components when appropriate. Save the design system to .agents/context/DESIGN_SYSTEM.md. Create a detailed, dependency-ordered implementation plan in .agents/plans/ with affected pages, reusable components, acceptance criteria, visual consistency checks, responsive requirements, and testing tasks. If useful, reference the supplied screenshots in the plan using their actual available paths; never invent image file paths. Summarize the proposed design in everyday language and request approval before finalizing it. Do not implement or modify application UI code. Update .agents/progress/STATUS.md with the design planning status when appropriate. Once the design is approved, suggest /start-build to implement it.
